utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is Wednesday, and I welcome everyone here, notably Mr. Stringer, who is going to continue with his closing arguments. Mr. Stringer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel. May it please the Court, I'm going to be continuing with the Prosecution's submissions in respect of General Praljak. And the first subject for today, Mr. President, is it relates to General Praljak, his knowledge of and his responsibility for the HVO prison camps and the prisoners there. Regarding the HVO prison camps and the detention facilities where thousands of Muslim men, including many civilians, were held throughout his entire tenure as commander of the HVO Main Staff, Praljak makes two general assertions. First, he claims that he had no involvement in or responsibility for the camps or the prisoners. At trial, he claimed he didn't even know about them. Secondly, General Praljak makes certain meritless claims regarding the legal status under international humanitarian law of the Muslim prisoners who were arrested and imprisoned beginning on the 30th of June, 1993, and I'm going to address this legal issue first on the status of the prisoners. According to General Praljak, there were essentially two categories of prisoners. The first of these were the Muslim men who had been members of the HVO at the time of the ABiH offensive on the 30th of June, 1993. Praljak claims that the isolation of what he calls these traitors was legitimate and that these prisoners benefit from no protection under international law. He says in paragraph 84 of his brief: "The law of armed conflict does not protect members of the armed forces --" let me start that again: "The law of armed conflict does not protect members of the armed groups from acts of violence directed against them by their own forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is a background noise in the microphone. I don't know whether anyone. I seem to have been the only one who had it. Please proceed. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In addressing this issue, Mr. President, I'd note that both the Accused Petkovic and Coric take the same general position in their briefs, and so our position, our remarks on this applies to those accused as well. This issue is addressed in paragraphs 145 to 147 of the Prosecution brief. Even if the Trial Chamber finds that the Muslim prisoners who had been members of the HVO were neither prisoners of war under the Third Geneva Convention nor civilians enjoining protection under the Fourth Geneva Convention, that does not mean that they can be subjected to cruel treatment, violence, or forced to perform unlawful labour in dangerous confrontation-line positions. I've got a slide I'd like to put up now. On this question of status, Mr. President, the Prosecution position is that these Muslim prisoners who had been members of the HVO who were disarmed and arrested fall within the protection of Article 75 of Additional Protocol I, which provides in part: "Insofar as they are affected by a situation referred to in Article 1 of this protocol, persons who are in the power of a Party to the conflict and who do not benefit from more favourable treatment under the Conventions or under this Protocol shall be treated humanely in all circumstances and shall enjoy, as a minimum, the protection provided by this Article ..." Then Article 75 continues on in paragraph 2 to prohibit violence to the life, health, physical, mental well-being of the persons, et cetera. If the Trial Chamber concludes that this category of prisoners were neither prisoners of war nor civilians, they are following squarely within the protection and the standards that are provided here in Article 75 of Additional Protocol I. In addition, whether or not they participated in the ABiH offensive on the 30th of June, any Muslim members of the HVO who were disarmed and imprisoned were from that point forward, of course, hors de combat. Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions thus supplies a minimum level of protection for those prisoners and requires that they are to be treated humanely. We have Article -- we have Common Article 3 up on the slide, but I'm sure the Trial Chamber and everyone else is well familiar with the minimum standards of protection that it lays down for all persons hors de combat, and that certainly applies to the Muslim men who had been members of the HVO, disarmed, and imprisoned by the HVO. Without doubt, the conditions of confinement, the mistreatment, and the forced labour on dangerous confrontation lines to which all the Muslim prisoners were subjected falls well below the minimum standards set out in Article 75 of AP I and Common Article 3. And so when the Defence assert that the Muslim prisoners who had been members of the HVO were fair game and they could be the target of cruel treatment and violence at the hands of their Croat HVO captors or that they could be forced to perform labour such as building trenches or building fortifications, they are wrong. In paragraph 85 of his brief, General Praljak attempts to justify the imprisonment of all the Muslim men of military age throughout HVO-controlled territory of Herceg-Bosna, stating: "In fact, it seems that all detainees," Praljak says, "possibly there were a few exceptions for whatever reason, were militarily-able men, mobilised or not, yet mobilised but without doubt in potential combatant status." Not surprisingly, General Praljak does not give us a citation to legal authority or any evidence that establishes that all of the prisoners were potential combat status. In fact, the large-scale and collective arrest and imprisonment of all the Muslim men of military age throughout all the HVO-held territories who were not members of the HVO constitutes the crime of unlawful imprisonment. Men in potential combatant status, as Praljak calls it, who are not actually combatants as defined by Article 4 of Geneva Convention 3, or Article 43 of Additional Protocol I are civilians. They're civilians under the Fourth Geneva Convention. Potential combatants cannot be detained collectively simply because they fall between the ages of 16 and 60. Detention can only be justified if made on an individual basis, if absolutely necessary because that person poses a particular risk or a security threat. The fact that a person is a male of military age is not sufficient justification to detain him, nor is ethnicity alone. What is relevant are a person's activities, knowledge, or qualifications, and so the mass arrest, the collective imprisonment of all Muslim men of military age, as was carried out in this case, solely on ethnic grounds was illegal. Even if there was some initial justification for imprisoning Muslim men because of concern that they might join the ABiH, any such justification for imprisonment or internment would only exist after an individual assessment of the risk of that prisoner, that individual, the risk of his joining forces or otherwise presenting a security risk. On this point we refer the Trial Chamber to Articles 5, 41 to 43 of Geneva Convention 4, as well as much of the jurisprudence already well established in this Tribunal as from the Celebici case and the Kordic cases. As the Celebici Trial Chamber stated, the fact that an individual is male and of military age should not necessarily justify detention. Mr. President, we also refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 150 to 153 and 308 to 322 of the Prosecution final brief where we apply the duty recognised in Celebici, the Celebici appeals case, the duty to release prisoners who do not pose a legitimate security risk or for whom these procedural guarantees have not been granted. The evidence in this case establishes that the accused did not adhere to a procedure for determining what individuals might pose a security threat so that those who did not could be released. The one individual prisoner assessment that did occur related to Muslim prisoners who gained release by procuring letters of guarantee promising that they would leave with their families from Herceg-Bosna altogether if they were released from imprisonment. I will address this issue in greater detail in my closing remarks tomorrow concerning the accused Mr. Coric. Despite Praljak's claim to the contrary, then, the collective arrest and imprisonment of Muslim civilian men of military age without regard to whether individuals among them posed a security threat and in the absence of a prompt review resulting in the release of those who did not, this was illegal. Furthermore, all prisoners, regardless of status as POW, Muslim, HVO members, or civilian, were, as I've already indicated, subjected to cruel and inhumane treatment and were sent regularly in large numbers to perform unlawful forced labour on the confrontation lines. There is no justification for subjecting any prisoners to these forms of criminal conduct, whatever their status under international humanitarian law. When he testified, General Praljak made a number of false statements regarding the HVO camps and the prisoners held there. On the 25th of August, 2009, he testified claiming that he didn't know even of General Petkovic's 30 June, 1993, order to arrest, isolate, detain all the Muslim men of military age. Praljak testified that he didn't know about that when he took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July. He said he was not informed. He did not know that the HVO was holding these prisoners in HVO detention facilities like the Heliodrom and Dretelj throughout Herceg-Bosna. On the 2nd of September, 2009, General Praljak testified, this is on pages 44289 to 90, claiming that neither he nor the HVO Main Staff had any responsibility for prisoners, and he claimed that he didn't know what person or body was responsible for them. This was on cross-examination. I asked him: "Q. You've heard testimony, you've seen the documents, military investigative prison at Ljubuski. At any time during that period you were commanding the HVO Main Staff, did you know about Muslim men being held prisoner at Ljubuski?" The answer he says: "No." "Q. Now, you said you never went to the Heliodrom. Did you ever go to Dretelj, Gabela, or Ljubuski during 1993?" His answer was: "No." On the 25th of August, 2009, Praljak even went so far as to say that even if he had known about the camps he would not have done anything about them. "I wouldn't have done anything ... I had nothing to do with prisons. I had nothing to do with prisons. What should I have done?" Mr. President and Your Honours, this is the Prosecution case and position in respect of General Praljak and the HVO camps: Number one, Praljak did know of the arrest order issued by General Petkovic on the 30th of June to imprison all the Muslim males of military age, and he was fully aware of the fact that he had thousands of prisoners in HVO custody when he took command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, 1993. Second, he did know that the conditions in the HVO prisons and camps did not meet minimum standards when he took command, and information on this continued to come to him from many sources in the days and weeks following the 24th of July. Third, once he was on notice concerning the conditions in the camps, he had an obligation to ensure that the conditions were made right. Fourth, he continued to evade and ignore responsibility to the HVO prisons and prisoners even after Herceg-Bosna president, his Commander-in-Chief, Mate Boban, expressly delegated to Praljak and the Main Staff responsibility for ensuring proper conditions in the camps and proper treatment of prisoners. So going back to the first point, what did Praljak know at the time on or about the 30th of June and moving forward? I'd like to take the Trial Chamber to a tool that I've been using. We'll see how well it works for all of us in the courtroom. We call it a time map. We've plotted a lot of evidence that's obviously only been admitted. I don't know if we're able to see this on our screens. No? Okay. What we've done is to plot admitted evidence and testimony here, and we can see along the time-line the top half events taking place in respect of the HVO camps and the arrest campaign that began on the 30th of June. The bottom half of the time-line we've plotted General Praljak's whereabouts based upon either his testimony or the admitted evidence. And what this tells us is that -- and I'll walk through the chronology just briefly. He was in the Prozor-Boksevica area on the 30th of June at the day, the time when the ABiH attack occurred and when the subsequent order went out to arrest and isolate all of the men. What we can first do is go to P03026 which is one of the exhibits noted on the time-line for the 30th of June, P03026. On the 30th of June Praljak was with operative zone commander Zeljko Siljeg at the HVO forward command post in Prozor. If he wasn't physically present with Siljeg there, he was in contact with Siljeg in that area. In an a communication that Siljeg sent on that day to Stojic and Petkovic, Siljeg stated on the 30th of June that he had familiarised Brada with the report from Mostar, with the conversation between Pasalic and Halilovic and with the command issued by the head of the Defence Department and the president of the HVO HZ-HB. That would have been the call to arms, if you will, or the mobilisation order issued by Mr. Stojic and the communications sent out by Mr. Prlic. Praljak obviously knew all significant aspects of the HVO response to the ABiH offensive of that day. P03246. Let me just take a brief moment, Mr. President. Sorry, Mr. President. I'm being informed -- it may be the registrar has taken something away from us by using e-court. If we could just take it back so we could use Sanction which is what we're using for the exhibits and also the time map programme, which is a different one. Sorry about that. Moving to P03246. On the 6th of July, we see that Praljak remained active in the highest levels of the HVO leadership during the first week of this period, July. On the 6th, Petkovic ordered that Praljak would be a part of the operation command or operation team assembled to organise combat activities as part of what was called Operation Boksevica. So he was still very present and very active, and in our submission, very well informed of the events taking place during the first week of July. In his testimony on the 26th of May, 2009, Praljak stated that he remained in the Boksevica area fighting until the 9th of July, when they pulled out. Praljak then went to see Mate Boban. As he said in his testimony, this is on page 40778 of the transcript: "Then I went to see Mate Boban. I discussed the whole situation with him. I think I had a brief meeting with Mr. Petkovic -- or, rather, that's not what I think. I know that we met." He continues then that he spoke to Mr. Stojic and that evening spent the night in that area, cleaned up at Mr. Stojic's place, and then left the following morning to go to Zagreb, which we say then would have been on the 11th of July. So from the 30th of June till the 11th of July when he left to return to Zagreb, the evidence, it's our submission, shows that Praljak would have been very well aware and was in full contact with all of the leading figures in the region and would very well have known about the widespread arrest campaign that was taking place during the first 11 days of July. P09470 is a video-clip of an interview that General Praljak gave to the BBC as part of "The Death of Yugoslavia." He tells us about his conversation with Mr. Stojic on, what we say, would have been the 11th of July or the 10th just before he leaves to return to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "So during the disarmament process when the camps started when people had to be put somewhere, I said as I was leaving, there was a short interregnum when I was not there, I remember that I said to Mr. Bruno Stojic, who was defence minister, 'Bruno take good care not to do something we would be ashamed of.' He told me that as regards our prison at Heliodrom, which was under my jurisdiction, I could be sure that they would do everything possible to prevent anything unpleasant. Of course, one knew that some unpleasant things would happen because we were not able very much to control things, although it could -- and what was down there was not under military control. It was simply a civilian part. That is how they set it up. Upon my return, I understood from what the people had started saying already that the camps looked bad. Fortunately, Mr. Sakota came and he used his personal authority to oppose some local bosses and ensure ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Upon his return he started hearing that the camps looked bad. Praljak would clearly have been aware of the building international media coverage surrounding the release of a group of emaciated Muslim prisoners from the Dretelj camp on the 28th of August, 1993. French television broadcast these images just a few days after prisoners released from Dretelj had been moved to ABiH-held territory near Jablanica. This is P00977B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. This is TV5, TV5, French TV coverage from the 31st of August, 1993. This was big news. P04640. At the time when the media coverage of the Dretelj prisoners that we've just seen, Praljak was in the Citluk HVO headquarters south of Mostar. So this is P04640. Okay. At the time of the media coverage, Praljak was in the Citluk headquarters, about 13 kilometres, we say, from Capljina municipality and the Dretelj camp itself where he had issued a number of orders related to events occurring throughout Herceg-Bosna, including issuing orders to, for example, the Zepce Brigade. Praljak clearly knew that he had big problems with the HVO camps to deal with at this period of time. P04716. On the next day, Praljak issued a pass. Media inquiries continued to put him on notice of problems in the HVO camps. He granted this pass to a German television crew to enter the Gabela camp. He issued this pass from the HVO Citluk headquarters a short distance from Capljina where the Gabela prison was located. In his testimony on the 2nd of September, 2009, General Praljak told us that he never even went. He never went to Gabela or Dretelj even after what we say was overwhelming information putting him on notice of the conditions there. P04841. These are minutes of the government meeting, the HVO HZ-HB meeting of the 6th of September. By early September conditions in the camps had become so widely known and such a political liability to the Herceg-Bosna leadership and these accused, they were forced to acknowledge the unlawful conditions in meetings with the Defence Department, that was on the 2nd of September, and in this meeting on the 6th. Here the Prlic government denied responsibility for conditions in the camps, but nonetheless decided it was necessary to improve conditions, to avoid the situation being used in ways that are adverse to the political and other interests of the HR HB. Clearly the illegality of what was happening in the camps was well-known to the Herceg-Bosna leadership. It was also well-known to Praljak. P10924. On the following day, the 7th of September, Reuters Deutschland reported on the release that day of the report of human UN human rights rapporteur Mazowiecki which, among other things, reported on the HVO camps. According to this both Mazowiecki and UNHCR were reporting the mistreatment of Muslim prisoners in these camps. There is an explicit reference to Gabela here, as well as imprisonment of men in aircraft hangars which, of course, is a clear reference to the Dretelj camp. The article continues: "According to the Mazowiecki report, in the town of Gabela south of Capljina, men were locked up in aircraft hangars, 16 prisoners survived on daily rations of a cup of watery soup and 650 grams of bread." It continues: "The UNHCR spokesman Ray Wilkinson demanded in Sarajevo to put utmost pressure on Croats for maintaining two detention camps in the southern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It says: "However, General Slobodan Praljak, commander of Bosnian Croats, declared that his soldiers were no longer holding any prisoners of war. Aid organisations and journalists are free to visit the ... camps." Praljak cynically concealed the fact that the HVO was, in fact, holding hundreds if not thousands of Muslim civilian men at this time, claiming to the UNHCR that the HVO was not holding any prisoners of war. The Trial Chamber will recall the testimony and the expert report submitted by General Andrew Pringle of the British Army. His expert report is P09549. In paragraph 77 he states: "If prisoners of war are handed over to another body, it is the responsibility of those handing them over to ensure that the receiving body complies and understands their responsibilities in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Moreover, if it becomes apparent that the prisoners of war, having been handed over to another body, are not being so treated, the original captors are beholden to take the prisoners of war back under their authority." On the 25th of August, 2009, at page 43784 of the transcript, Praljak told us about the handing over of prisoners to the military police. In support of his claim that neither he nor the HVO staff, Main Staff, were responsible for the prisoners, Praljak indicated that the prisoners were the responsibility of the military police. He said: "... whenever someone is captured, it was one's duty to hand over the prisoners to the military police." The evidence indeed shows that it was the military police under the command of Coric which exercised daily control over the prisoners by providing security at the HVO camps and administering or facilitating such things as the HVO forced labour programme, but the evidence establishes that even by the time he returned to take command of the HVO Main Staff on the 24th of July, 1993, Praljak knew there were serious problems regarding conditions in the camps. As the evidence I have just summarised shows, within weeks of his return, the highly publicised release of prisoners from Dretelj made world news. Conditions in the camps were reported by the UN Special Rapporteur Mazowiecki. Journalists were asking Praljak for access. The evidence establishes beyond a reasonable doubt that Praljak knew that the Muslim prisoners, having been arrested and handed over to the military police, were not being treated in accordance with international humanitarian law. As Pringle tells us, and this is confirmed by the Tribunal's own jurisprudence in the Mrksic case, once he had reason to know that the prisoners were not being held in proper conditions, Praljak had a duty to take them under his authority and ensure they receive proper treatment. Instead, he ignored the problem and his responsibility. Any doubt or ambiguity about Praljak's personal responsibility for the prisoners and the camps, as commander of the HVO Main Staff, is laid to rest when he was specifically directed by Mate Boban to take responsibility for ensuring lawful conditions in the camps on the 15th of September, 1993. This is P05104. In item 3, Mate Boban requires that the conditions required by international law be introduced in the prisoner of war detention centres and that the prisoners be treated in accordance with international standards. Item 7 specifically directs the Main Staff not only to inform subordinates about the order but also to provide professional help in its implementation. When General Praljak was asked about this order from Boban during his cross-examination, he acknowledged receiving the order, although he testified that he did not fully transmit the order down the chain of command. Refusing to acknowledge that Boban had specifically directed the Main Staff and Praljak, together with the Defence Department to ensure the proper treatment of prisoners as set out in items 3 and 7, Praljak, on his own, decided that three -- items 3, 4, and 5 did not apply to him. He expressly refused to carry out his obligations in respect to the prisoners and prisons even after being ordered to do so by his Commander-in-Chief. And so again we see Praljak refusing to exercise any authority or to take the slightest action to improve the situation for prisoners in the camps. The result of this, as the Trial Chamber knows, was that the Muslim prisoners continued to suffer in the camps for additional weeks and months. Unlawful forced labour on the front lines, a well entrenched and widespread practice employed at all of the HVO detention facilities, continued unabated after the 15th of September. On the topic of forced labour, Mr. President, in paragraph 83 of his brief Praljak claims that he never ordered forced labour and that he in fact prohibited the practice. The evidence shows otherwise. P04260. Praljak relies entirely on this exhibit, an order that he issued on the 17th of August, 1993, directing that prisoners in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf be withdrawn from the tasks they have been given by 1800 hours. He directed that the Rama Brigade SIS and the military police be responsible for the safe return and security of these prisoners in prison. This document tells us, of course, that Praljak knew the prisoners were being used to perform forced labour and that he was in a position to exercise control over the prisoners, the military police, and the SIS personnel in Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, in respect of prisoners. Using the language of the Mrksic appeal judgement, Praljak, like all of the accused in this case, was an agent of the detaining power. He was among those having custody of these prisoners. These prisoners were in his hands. On the 2nd of June, 2009, during his testimony, when asked by Judge Trechsel whether he had ordered an investigation related to the use of these forced labourers, Praljak stated that he had not, because he lacked the investigative resources. He said that it was up to the SIS to do something about the practice. There is no evidence of any other written order by Praljak prohibiting the use of prisoners for forced labour or of him referring this practice for investigation or pursuing disciplinary measures against those engaged in the practice. P04285. On the same day that Praljak issued his order that the prisoners be withdrawn from work, in a classic example of an effective working chain of command regarding the use of prisoners for labour, the commander of the HVO Rama Brigade reported directly to Praljak that his order on the withdrawal of prisoners had been carried out. This shows the brigade and not only the SIS and the military police was involved with prisoners and reported to Praljak about them. Praljak's order of 17 August does not apply to any location outside of the north-west Herzegovina operative zone. Indeed, the use of prisoners for forced labour continued in Prozor, as in all other locations under HVO control, where the HVO needed labourers to perform dangerous work on the front lines. The Trial Chamber will hear more on the use of prisoners from the Heliodrom for illegal forced labour as part of my submissions on Valentin Coric. I'm going to refer now to P04307. It's an ECMM report, so we can't show it outside the courtroom, but I can refer to it. It's dated the 19th of August, 1993, ECMM, just two days after Praljak's order that the prisoners be withdrawn from work in Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. They report on their visit with 167 Muslim prisoners being held at the tech school in Prozor. The HVO operative zone command, according to this report, naming Siljeg, stated they were not prisoners of war but men between 16 and 60 that were being kept there in order to control them. "They are being used as forced labour by the HVO to dig trenches on the front lines in the Gornji Vakuf area..." The report continues: "... some have died as a result of this work." Mr. President, I'd like to look at one other time-line briefly that relates to this issue. On the date of this ECMM report that I've just read from, which is the 19th of August, 1993, if we go to that area, we can see that Praljak was in the Prozor forward command post headquarters on the 17th of August. That's the day he issued the order on withdrawal. He was there on the 16th. He was also there on the 21st, according to an order he issued that day before apparently then moving on to the south to Citluk and Mostar where he issued other orders on that day from that location. So what we know is that Praljak was right in the HVO Prozor headquarters at the time that the ECMM was taking these reports from detainees about the forced labour that was taking place. P04877. This order was issued by Praljak's trusted subordinate operative zone commander Zeljko Siljeg and makes clear that the practice of forced labour was alive and well in Prozor at the very time that Praljak was there commanding HVO units. Here Siljeg issues a patently unlawful order regulating the use of Balijas for engineering work on the first line of defence. It's important to note again, we see the brigade in the operative zone directly subordinate to Praljak exerting direct authority over Muslim prisoners for purposes of forced labour. Item 3 very clearly shows that Siljeg anticipated Muslim prisoners would be wounded and killed while performing this labour as he directed reports on the number of wounded or killed prisoners be made for record-keeping purposes. This order also makes it clear that the HVO operative zone command in Prozor, at the very same time that Praljak was present there, was issuing orders regulating the use of prisoners for forced labour. This is not surprising given the fact that it was the HVO armed forces, the brigade's operative zones, and ultimately the Main Staff commanded by General Praljak that were the beneficiaries of the forced labour programme. It's also not surprising given Praljak's statements to this Trial Chamber that he would do whatever it takes to win the war at all costs, even if that meant subjecting the Muslim population to greater crime. We go back to the time-line for the 8th of September, the date of this order on regulating the use of Balijas for forced labour. We see that also on that same day Praljak was present in the Citluk forward command post headquarters of the HVO where he issued an order in evidence as 3D02759, a transmission sent from Prozor down to Citluk, asking them to send some Motorolas. P09661, another ECMM report we can't show outside. On that day, ECMM reported that they visited the HVO POW camp at Prozor. They report: "This camp is not a military detention camp but a detention camp for civilian internees. The camp is located at the town's technical school, 100 metres from the HVO headquarters. There were 226 civilians imprisoned at the camp. Almost every day they are digging trenches in the area of Trnovaca. At least four detainees have, during the digging ... in the absence of the camp guards the internees mentioned that they thought that between 40 and 60 people had been killed working on the trenches." Mr. President, General Praljak was very regularly at the headquarters in Prozor. As he told the Trial Chamber, he devoted the lion's share of his attention and energies into that area. The Prosecution submits that the evidence shows beyond a reasonable doubt that Praljak knew of and approved the systematic use of the Muslim civilian detainees to perform this labour in the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf theatre of operations. A couple final points in terms of his control over prisoners. 3D00981. This is a communication or a special report sent to Praljak from Prozor and operative zone Commander Siljeg. Item number 4, he says: "The representatives of EC," that would be the European Community, we say the ECMM, "presented their problems today. "A) VP, military police, Rama, does not allow them to visit Hodza in Prozor." Item C: "They want to visit the prisoners of war in Prozor." 3D00979. The following day, 23rd of September, Praljak issues this response from the Citluk headquarters where he's located on that day, telling Siljeg: "A. Allow EZ," European Community, "to visit Hodza." Hodza being in all likelihood the imam or the Muslim priest in Prozor. And then also authorising item C; that is, authorising ECMM to visit the prisoners in Prozor. So again, this tells us despite his sworn testimony that he didn't know about any prisoners, evidently not even those prisoners in Prozor at the tech school that were being held 100 metres from the HVO headquarters there. Praljak exerts, in fact, direct authority over these prisoners, and he has full knowledge of them. Mr. President, while we're on the issue of forced labour, I should make a few brief comments about P06937. It's dated the 8th of November, 1993. It's an order from Mostar bearing signatures of a Mijo Jelic and also bearing the signature of what we say is General Slobodan Praljak. The Trial Chamber will recall the Praljak Defence and General Praljak asserts that this document, his signature on it, is a forgery. We point out that when the Trial Chamber looks at the original document itself, it will, of course, find the stamp of the HVO Main Staff on the document, as well as signatures and all the necessary stamps one would expect of a legitimate authentic HVO document. The Trial Chamber will also recall P04 -- excuse me. P02642, an HVO log-book which on paragraph -- on page 17, item 407, expressly records the order of Jelic and Praljak approving the use of prisoners for forced labour. So the document is recorded in the HVO's own log-books. In addition on this point, Mr. President, P05873 is a piece of evidence worth bearing in mind. It's an order issued on the 14th of October, 1993, by General Petkovic. He issues it to all brigades of the HVO south-east Herzegovina operative zone, and in item 1 he prohibits the removal of prisoners to perform any kind of labour. Item 2, he says: "Should such activity nevertheless be allowed, the permit shall be issued by the HVO Main Staff." So the Prosecution position, Mr. President, is that Praljak's signature on 6937, the alleged forgery, is in full agreement, in fact, with the order issued by General Petkovic on the 14th of October. In other words, Petkovic ordered that approval for prisoner release in the south-east operative zone has to be approved or the permits obtained by Main Staff. Praljak was indeed still on the 8th of November, the Chief of the HVO Main Staff. He was present in the Main Staff on the 8th of November, and in signing off on the request to use prisoners that day, he provided the necessary permit as required by the earlier Petkovic order. As the Trial Chamber knows, Praljak resigned his position and left from the HVO Citluk headquarters on the morning of the 9th of November, 1993. He testified that he arrived in Citluk on the previous evening when he issued his report for an order on the events at Stupni Do. Knowing that he was leaving the HVO and Herceg-Bosna altogether on the following day, the Prosecution submits it was perfectly reasonable to assume that Praljak would have first gone to the HVO Defence sector headquarters in Mostar on the 8th of November on his way down to Citluk to say his good-byes. We assert that's when he signed off on this approval for the prisoners to be used for forced labour. Mr. President, the Prosecution submits that all of this shows the alleged forgery, P06937, is an authentic document. Given the widespread use of prisoners throughout all areas under HVO control, as well as Praljak's full awareness and control over events in these areas, he unquestionably knew of and approved the practice of using Muslim prisoners for forced labour. General Praljak will be the first one to tell you of the HVO's mobilisation problems and the difficulties they had in keeping soldiers on the front lines. The Trial Chamber has seen and heard extensive evidence of that throughout the trial. If General Praljak was willing to deploy the military police into battle rather than using them to prevent crimes, he was certainly willing to use prisoners to fortify the trenches on the front lines. The massive use of Muslim prisoners, regardless of their status as civilian, prisoner of war, or a detained Muslim HVO, during the time that Praljak was commander of the Main Staff is, in the Prosecution's submission, beyond question. These prisoners as labourers were a key component of Praljak's win the war at all cost command strategy. Your Honours, I would like to devote the final few minutes of my submissions to a discussion of General Praljak's responsibility for the ethnic cleansing of entire communities of Muslims from areas in Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, and Prozor in August of 1993, during this time that General Praljak was in command of the HVO Main Staff. Now, I'd like to first return to an exhibit that was used during the cross-examination of one of the Defence witnesses. It's admitted into evidence -- it's actually two exhibits; IC00833 and 834. We can blow-up 833 so that everybody can see. The Trial Chamber will recall -- the Trial Chamber may recall that the data contained in these tables was discussed with the Defence witness Martin Raguz, who had been with the HVO office of displaced persons and refugees, ODPR. The data in the table, the numbers, come from reports prepared by ODPR, and the data had been provided by ODPR to a representative of an international humanitarian organisation that was working in the region during the fall of 1993. And, Mr. President, if we could briefly go into private session. I'd like to make one additional remark about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The data contained in these tables, ODPR's own data, confirms what the extensive evidence shows regarding the ethnic cleansing of Muslim communities in Ljubuski, Capljina, and Stolac. While General Praljak directly notes that the HVO cleansing of Stolac began prior to 24 July 1993, when he took command of the HVO Main Staff, the evidence shows that this ethnic cleansing campaign in that region continued unabated after Praljak took command on the 24th. The evidence proves, for example, the Prosecution submits, that thousands of Muslim, Bosnian women, children, and elderly were driven from Capljina town and other parts of that municipality on the 23rd of August, 1993. They were rounded up, driven from their homes, and loaded onto buses where they were transported first to the collection site at the silos where many were mistreated and they were forced to leave behind all their belongings, and then finally loaded onto buses and expelled by the HVO out into ABiH-held territory. In Ljubuski municipality during the latter half of August 1993, the Bosnian Muslim populations in Gradska, Vitina, and other parts of Ljubuski municipality were deported. Entire communities of Muslims vanished from these areas. In July, August, and September of 1993, terror reigned. Thousands were removed from these municipalities by the HVO while Praljak was commander of the Main Staff. Getting back to the tables, according to the ODPR data, from a pre-war population of nearly 1600 people, the population of Muslim residents in Ljubuski was reduced by some 50 per cent. ODPR reports a similar 50 per cent reduction in the Muslim resident population of Capljina during the period between September and October of 1993. In Stolac, the Muslim population was reduced from 8.101 to 0, according to ODPR's own data. The other table, IC00834, relates not to long-time Muslim residents, people who had always lived in these areas. 834 refers to the refugee populations that have come in. The Muslim refugees, indeed, the displaced persons driven into these areas, largely from the east by Serb armed forces, they fared even worse. According to ODPR, all Muslim refugees living in the municipalities of Ljubuski, Capljina, and Stolac had been removed by October of 1993, and you can see that by the zeros that are in these boxes concerning the data kept by ODPR. The Trial Chamber will note that throughout the same period the proportion of Croat residents remains unchanged. That's in the first table, 833. We see in the table 834 that according to ODPR's data, thousands of Croat refugees from elsewhere arrived in this area to replace and did replace the Muslims who had, in the Prosecution's submission, been removed. General Praljak knew about the events taking place all the way up in Vares, Stupni Do. He was issuing orders and having communications with the HVO Zepce Brigade farther to the north and the east. He knew the situation facing Croat refugees from places like Konjic and Bugojno. He wrote about all that extensively in his brief, and yet he did not know about what happened to the Muslim populations in Ljubuski, Stolac, Capljina? Impossible. The large-scale expulsion and deportation during Praljak's tenure as commander of the HVO Main Staff was, of course, not limited to these municipalities. The remaining Muslim population in Prozor, which by early August 1993 had been crammed into houses in Podgrade, Lapsunj, and Duge was finally expelled by the HVO. It bears noting that the Muslims who were brutally expelled from their homes or from these areas while Praljak was commander in August and September were the most defenseless of civilians. All of the men had already been arrested and placed in the HVO camps and detention facilities throughout the region. When we speak about the expulsions and the removal of communities of Muslims from these regions during August, September, July of 1993, we're talking about the elderly, the women, the children, those who'd left alone to fend for themselves after the men had already been taken away and imprisoned. I'm going to go back to P04307. The ECMM report of their visit to the detainees and their findings in other travels in that region on the 19th of August. This is P04307. This is a report. "We have also been informed that the Muslims in Prozor have all been moved to three areas in the region: Podgrade, Lapsunj, and Duge. The last two places V2 will visit tomorrow. In Podgrade there was 1.760 old men, women, and children. The houses in the area were filled with a minimum of 30 occupants each. Conditions are poor but there is sufficient food provided by Merhamet. A doctor visits the area once every two weeks. The Muslims are not allowed to leave this area. There are indications that HVO soldiers come into the area at night and rape the women they wish. All the men between 16 and 60 are gone. They are very frightened as to their future. Many are DPs," displaced persons, "from other parts of the country. V2," that's the reporting unit of ECMM here, "V2 expects to find the same situation in the other two Muslim areas." Can we briefly go back into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber might recall what ultimately happened to these Muslims from these villages in the Prozor area. The Trial Chamber might recall the testimony of Witness BK. After witnessing the execution and the immolation, that is, the burning of her father at Mount Tolovac, Witness BK and her family were bused to Podgradze, a village where approximately 6.000 Muslims were staying. Upon their arrival, they took up residence in a house with approximately 90 other Muslims. At the end of August, Witness BK and her family, along with 6.000 Muslim women, children, and elders, were forced out of Podgradze by the HVO soldiers. They were given five minutes to pack up and to get out. They were taken away, ultimately bused to Kucani, and then moved across from there into the ABiH-held territory. So we know exactly the fate of the people that the ECMM was reporting about on the 19th of August. We know that indeed at the end of August they were expelled from this area, driven out by the HVO. In his brief Praljak claims he did not know about the expulsion of Muslims from these municipalities, that he never received any reports or information about these events. He does not mention or address the deportation of the Muslim population from Ljubuski at all in his brief. The evidence shows that Praljak moved freely throughout all HVO-controlled territory during the entire time that these crimes were taking place. He moved easily from Gornji Vakuf to Prozor, to Mostar, to Citluk, issuing orders from all of these locations and demonstrating his knowledge and familiarity with all significant events in this region. And it's not a big region. It is impossible that Praljak was not aware of the significant HVO assets, men, equipment, logistics that were deployed in order to accomplish the expulsion of the Muslim community, from Capljina, for example, or from Prozor at the end of August. The removal of 6.000 people in one day takes a lot of equipment and a lot of organising. I'd like to quickly move to IC0062. It's a map. I'm not going to dwell on this because we always have arguments about scale on maps that are shown on the screens here, but it's just worth recalling the region we're talking about, particularly Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski in relation to the HVO Citluk headquarters. Mr. President, I've got the mouse over the area that I've been talking about here, Stolac, Ljubuski, Citluk. There's Mostar. Citluk is in this area. These are all very, very close to each other and, of course, are well within areas fully under HVO control. There's no question of the HVO being challenged in their actions with regard to the civilian populations in these areas. The Trial Chamber's invited to review the maps, to consider the very short distances involved in all of these areas, and how that impacts Praljak's knowledge and his awareness of all of the events that we've been talking about. In any event, even though he claims he didn't know about these events, we do have a good idea of what Praljak would have done about these events, and we have a good explanation of why he, in fact, didn't do anything about these many crimes. P0 -- excuse me P10958. This is an article, an interview given by General Praljak some years later, in April of 2004. The Trial Chamber may recall he was asked about this, these comments, on cross-examination. This is what Praljak said when he was talking about what happened to the Muslims in Stolac: "Stolac? There is nothing wrong there. What happened in the concentration camp should not have happened in such a way, and it is a real crime. But to disarm a soldier in battle, that is what I signed for tomorrow. What happened later on - I would not sign for. Anyway, I was the one who let journalists in Stolac! And then after a month and a half they expelled women and children from the town. I would award the one who did it with a medal, because he saved them from the revenge of the refugees from Central Bosnia. If they wanted to expel them, they would have done it immediately - in this way, they did not expel them, they saved them." Mr. President, General Praljak himself denies that he had any responsibility to protect these people, the vulnerable civilian Muslim populations, the women, the children, and elderly that were left on their own throughout Herceg-Bosna after all the men of military age had been arrested and taken away. As he claims on page 124 of his brief: "As a commander of HVO Main Staff, Praljak had no duties and/or authority to impose law and order in areas out of the battle zone. The HVO civil authorities were duty-bound for maintenance of law and order." On this he is wrong. The fact is, Your Honours, these areas that I have been describing the last few minutes, Prozor, Stolac, Capljina, Ljubuski, as well as all the other areas held by the HVO armed forces while Praljak was commander of the HVO Main Staff, were occupied territory under international law. As the commanding general of that occupied territory, Praljak was indeed duty-bound to protect all the civilians regardless of their ethnicity. He turned his back on the civilian populations in those areas just as he turned his back on the Muslim men in the HVO prisons and camps. The Trial Chamber will find the Prosecution's submissions on occupied territory in its brief. I won't repeat those, other than to say that a territory is occupied when the occupying power has rendered the occupied authorities incapable of functioning publicly or of controlling the area, and is in a position to exercise its own control over that territory. That test is amply met in this case in virtually all of the areas where crimes were committed against the Muslim civilian population by the HVO. In places like Stolac, Capljina, West Mostar, Prozor, for example, there was no legitimate civilian authority linked to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in place. Those legitimate government authorities had long since been pushed out as part of the HVO power grab that served as a precursor to the HVO military takeover that followed. The HVO and its armed forces were able to easily and swiftly exert its authority and control over the areas we say form occupied territory. We see the evidence of this in the ease with which the HVO arrested and imprisoned all the Muslim men throughout the occupied territories beginning on 30 June, 1993. We see this in the ease with which the HVO was able to round up, mistreat at will, and ultimately deport the vulnerable Muslim civilian populations who remained outside the HVO camps. We see this in the unchecked expulsion of the Muslims from their flats in West Mostar, the appropriation of their flats by the HVO, and the expulsion of those Muslims across the river into East Mostar. The Trial Chamber, recalling the thousands of Muslims left in Prozor who were rounded up, held in the houses, in the villages I've just described a few minutes earlier, we see this in decisions. I say we see occupied territory. We see the HVO's full ability and capacity to exert its own authority in these territories. We see this in the decisions such as those taken by Praljak to remove military and civilian policemen from their policing duties and to put them into combat to fight against the legitimate army and authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, placing the Muslim populations in even greater peril. And then, of course, these are the scores -- there are the scores of decisions, decrees, regulations issued by the Prlic government purporting to regulate all aspects of life in Herceg-Bosna. None of this could happen unless the HVO had indeed rendered the legitimate authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina incapable of functioning in these areas. None of this could happen unless the HVO was in a position to impose its authority over the Muslim populations in these areas, and it did. Praljak as commander of the HVO armed forces after July 24, as well as his co-accused, Milivoj Petkovic, for the period of time prior to July 24th, 1993. Praljak had a duty to protect all the civilians from crime, terror, persecution, and all the other crimes they suffered throughout the HVO's campaign to establish Herceg-Bosna. Praljak's failure to honour this duty, his failure to make even the slightest attempt to protect the civilians in these occupied territories, is not just relevant because it bears on his liability for aiding and abetting. His failure to honour this duty to protect even the most defenceless people in Herceg-Bosna tells us that he accepted that persecution, deportation, and all the other crimes that go with it committed against these people were a necessary means of achieving a separate, autonomous territory where Croats would be in the majority. What we see in Stolac, Ljubuski, Capljina, Prozor, West Mostar, and throughout all these areas held by the HVO under Praljak's command is his legacy, the legacy of Slobodan Praljak. Mission accomplished at least in those places. And as a theatre man with a flare for the dramatic, what better exit from the centre stage could there have been for Slobodan Praljak than for the HVO's guns to finally bring the Stari Most, the famous Old Bridge crashing down into the Neretva River on the very morning that he left the HVO's Citluk headquarters and returned home to Zagreb. Mr. President and Your Honours, the Prosecution will have some additional final submissions to make with respect to General Praljak. That completes my remarks at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, we're glad to see you, and I welcome you, and you have the floor, even though you're hiding behind the rostrum.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in the courtroom. Kim West for the Office of the Prosecutor. I will be delivering the Prosecutor's closing argument in response to the Petkovic Defence brief. The accused argues that he was not a political person, that he had no involvement in the HVO plan to permanently remove and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims in Herceg-Bosna. This argument appears in numerous paragraphs of his brief, most clearly in paragraph 41. You'll see that on the screen. That he was never politically engaged. And in paragraph 43, he did not attend any meeting where the goals, programmes, policies, operations, and strategies of the HZ-HB might have been discussed. Petkovic equates the notion of political involvement as evidencing JCE intent, and with this the Prosecution agrees. However, the Prosecution does not agree that Petkovic was merely a titular head of the military. Petkovic was the military general in command and control of the armed forces, and in using that position he executed the Herceg-Bosna JCE, but he was also a leading member of the hierarchy whose input and skill was invaluable in developing and facilitating the plan. The first issue I will address is Petkovic's role in creation of Herceg-Bosna and his significant contribution to the JCE. In the next slide you will see Defence Annex 9, supporting his position that he was not politically engaged. It is a listing of governmental meetings where his attendance is recorded only four times. Now, I will not suggest to you that Petkovic attended such meetings daily or that he was an active participant in the daily execution of the government. Petkovic was too busy commanding the armed forces to do that. However, it is the government's position that Petkovic attended and participated in critical government meetings where the direction of the JCE was discussed. Four of those meetings are now found in the following slide. These are four meetings that Petkovic did not mention in his brief. The first, on July 3rd, you'll be familiar with. This is the meeting in which the decree of armed forces was adopted. Petkovic's attendance at that important meeting is not surprising. The August 1993 meeting, the last meeting, where the republic was commenced, is also a significant and defining moment in the JCE, a moment that Petkovic would not have missed. Now, as shown on the next slide, the December 1992 meeting was also very important. This is a Defence Department meeting. Petkovic discussed the set-up of the army and how best to structure it. And the minutes say: "Petkovic considers that it would be suffice to provide for six generals in the Armed Forces." This is a very high-level meeting chaired by Accused Stojic, and an important decision was entrusted to a man who after consideration thought six generals was enough. The Trial Chamber should ask itself what was the goal of the armed forces? Six generals was enough to do what? It is inconceivable that the person who headed the armed forces, the entity entrusted with executing the plan was not in on the plan itself. In the next slide, this is from the brief, the Defence claims that Petkovic was at none of the Presidential meetings where the political direction of the conflict was discussed. He participated in only one meeting of the HR HB delegation with Tudjman, and that was in relation to Stupni Do. Your Honours, this assertion is simply untrue. Petkovic did participate in at least two very important meetings in President Tudjman's office where the political direction of the conflict was discussed, and one of them is P02059. At this April 24th meeting in Tudjman's office, it lasted for four hours. It was a top-level discussion of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. It included two heads of state, their military leadership, their political lieutenants, as well as top international negotiators, and the first major item for business at this meeting was to hear the reports from Generals Petkovic and Halilovic regarding their discussions about military negotiations and the peace plan and a potential Joint Command. As he finished explaining his position, Petkovic himself noted the political implications for both sides. And that's found at page 10 of this report. You'll see it in front of you. He says: "I think that in this way command effectiveness would not suffer at all. In view of political implications for both sides, their soldiers would not be in any way subordinate position to the HVO ..." Your Honours, I would submit that this was an explicitly political discussion, and immediately after Petkovic's report, Tudjman and Izetbegovic remarked on exactly that. On page 11, Tudjman: "Thank you. It's obvious that it's a technical question at the military level, it's a political thing. "Izetbegovic: Ladies and gentlemen, I agree with President Tudjman. This is obviously a political issue." There were several more meetings that benefitted from Petkovic's attendance and significant participation, and you see them now before you. As regard to the first meeting in June of 1992, the Defence asserts the following at paragraph 537 in their brief: "Words of 'Croatian interest' and 'Croatian-held territory' that were written in this document, used in these documents, had the meaning that the territory was free, liberated of Serb forces. These words did not have any anti-Muslim meaning." Now, the Trial Chamber will well remember the cross-examination regarding this document, and I'm not going to reiterate our brief's analysis of Petkovic's unconvincing denial that this document isn't exactly what it plainly reads to be, but you will see at the bottom of this document the four issues that are -- the four facts that are at issue here, and the first is: "To put under control the remaining area of Croatian municipalities. "To secure and fortify the achieved line. "To carry out reorganisation of the existing HVO forces; and "To establish Croatian rule over all municipalities." The Defence would have you believe that the reasonable interpretation of those lines was merely to establish rule excluding the Serbs, that the rule would be somehow shared between the Muslims and the Croats, that each time this document says "Croat," it should be interpreted to somehow read "Croat and Muslim." I submit to you that that understanding is completely at odds with the plain language of the document, and this is a document that was signed by the accused himself. If the Trial Chamber needed more Petkovic documents evidencing that he was aware of the JCE and on board with it and significantly contributed to it, then we can look at the 1992 report where Petkovic reports on the Herceg-Bosna borders and how far along the HVO was in achieving their goal. And in the next slide you will see that document. This document is not mentioned in the Defence brief. It's mentioned in one of the annexes as a report allegedly issued by Petkovic, and this report is for the period of April to December 1992, and under the general conclusions on page 2, Petkovic writes: "Nowadays, HVO forces successfully hold under their control 90 per cent of the area mapped out as HZ-HB, and they are capable and ready to defend it ..." This is a document that you've seen, I believe, yesterday from Mr. Scott, but there's another interesting part of this report that I would like to show you, and this is on page 4. This is a clear reference to the philosophy, the political will of the army, the JCE that the army was fighting to implement, and here we have: "The defence of this area and unit commanding in most cases depends on 'ordinary' people who do not have military school -- excuse me, skills, but are dedicated to the ideas of the HZ-HB." Petkovic here refers to military men whose most important attribute is not their experience but their philosophical conviction to the ideas to the HZ-HB, men like Petkovic. It was his task to take over the territory and ensure that it was ruled by Croats only, that a new political social order was installed to the exclusion of Muslims. If we look at his tasks in the HVO, we see that to be the case. That is the next document on the screen in front of you. This is the book of rules on the operation of the armed services, and under number 1 it shows the tasks: "To protect and defend the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of HZ-HB," and "To defend the social set-up of HZ-HB as established by the Constitution." This document shows that the armed forces in defending the political system of the HZ-HB, they were clearly stating their allegiance to a new state with a whole new order, a new social set-up, and eventually that meant population transfers of Muslims out and Croats in to ensure Croat domination. As you heard, the Defence brief asserts that the accused did not participate in any political discussions with Tudjman in his office. I'd like now to look at the 5 November meeting in Split, and this comes just in the aftermath of Stupni Do. It was a gathering of Croat and Herceg-Bosna's top leaders, including Prlic, Petkovic, and Praljak, to discuss the problems of the Croat parastate in BiH, and in particular Stupni Do. And at page 4, Tudjman lays out their political goals, saying: "If the BiH union breaks up, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the autonomous province of Western Bosnia will be annexed to the republic ..." And also that, a little bit below: "Therefore, our policy has always been and will be to keep the Republic of Herceg-Bosna." On page 21, Tudjman also explained precisely what this policy meant in the short term for Petkovic and the HVO military, and he said: "The present situation demands the measures to be taken to strengthen the functioning of the authorities in this part of Herceg-Bosna and to defend the line in the north of Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca." This is clearly the application of a political philosophy to military tactics. The two go hand-in-hand. One cannot exist without the other. Petkovic could have not have led the army and not been part of the political will of which it was born. In the next slide we see the HVO policy of reverse ethnic cleansing was also discussed at this meeting, and it included moving the military along with the population. This is Prlic: "We must move closer to rounding off territories. As a government, last spring we defined both the proposal and the conclusions, even with regard to moving certain brigades from some areas, which would include moving the population from those areas and concentrating it in certain directions that we think could become and remain Croatian areas." Your Honours, this was an intensely political meeting where Petkovic is asked for his contribution. He is there surrounded by the Croatian president and other HVO leaders, but Petkovic comes to you now denying that he had a political bone in his body. The Defence you would have to believe, that Petkovic was merely an administrative assistant to Boban with no power or autonomy or decision-making power of his own. But if the Prosecution's allegations are true and Petkovic was a military and political leader in Herceg-Bosna, then the Trial Chamber should expect that at the time other people thought the same. The Trial Chamber should expect to have seen international figures meeting with the person they believed to be worthy of HVO decision-making capacity. The Trial Chamber should have seen other Herceg-Bosna leaders interacting with Petkovic in a manner keeping with his position as one of the Herceg-Bosna leaders. The person described by the Defence brief certainly would not have had a seat at the table in Geneva in January, negotiating a peace plan for the parties, nor would he have been meeting with Mladic discussing the two army's plans for co-operation, yet this is the very credible evidence before you. The next slide notes occasions when high-level officials mentioned Petkovic, revealing their understanding of his very important position in the HVO. In the first document, this is a July 2nd meeting, presidential meeting, where it reads: "And you two please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with the Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic, and ambassador Sancevic and their leaders there ..." And it goes on. The Trial Chamber will recall the grammatical defence offered by the accused to this document when he said that the placement of the comma excluded reference to him as one of the Herceg-Bosna leaders. I think the plain reading of this document shows the weakness of that explanation. The next document is April 27th, where Susak says at the meeting: "About BiH. I talked to Petkovic at about 1930 hours." This shows that Petkovic was a point person for all things Herceg-Bosna. The next meeting, 11 May: "8.00 tonight, General Petkovic, Morillon's deputy, and Halilovic met up there in Kiseljak. Morillon arrives at Medjugorje tonight to meet with Boban and Petkovic." Here you see Petkovic's participation in high-level meetings and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies. November 5th. This is a meeting we just talked about. Prlic says: "I think this meeting is extremely important. The highest-ranking officials of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are here ..." Petkovic was at that meeting and was referred to as one of those officials. And then we have a cite to his -- his testimony itself. And this was on cross-examination, and the question was: "Would you agree with me, wouldn't you, that you were more than just a political/military technocrat; you really were wearing a political hat as well as a military hat, weren't you? "A. No, I didn't have a political hat of any kind." And then when shown an article in which he said he felt more like a politician in that time, he replied in that article that it seemed to him that he was more politician than soldier. And he said -- he was asked: "That's what you said in the interview, isn't it?" His answer: "This does seem strange, this statement that I'm more politician than soldier. I don't really see myself as a politician." The accused did not deny that he more of a politician than soldier. He merely thought it was odd. What else can the Trial Chamber rely on in finding that Petkovic shared the intent to permanently remove and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats from Herceg-Bosna and join it as part of the Greater Croatia? I submit that the Trial Chamber should look at the ultimatums. The ultimatums and Petkovic's role in their issuance is important because it illustrates his commitment to Croatian-only rule in those areas claimed by Herceg-Bosna. The ultimatums were an attempt at a wholly unjustified grab for territory and power without any agreement by the other parties. But in reviewing this evidence, I ask that the Trial Chamber focus also on the evolution of Petkovic's position, particularly on the January ultimatum, what he said initially in his testimony, then in his cross, and now in his brief, and focus on whether the inconsistency and evolution of his position bears on the credibility of his testimony. I am not suggesting that the accused need carry any burden at all. That burden is solely and always on the Prosecution, but I think the evolution of Petkovic's rationalisations for the ultimatum is helpful to the Trial Chamber in its own determination as to the credibility of his testimony. So we see in paragraph 536, this is the brief on the ultimatum, and in it, it says: "The order is purely military in character and is consistent with the instructions given to him by his government. It was not for him ... to second-guess the nature and reasons for his superior's orders." So the Defence position in the brief is that his superiors told him to do it and so he did it. There's no analysis of the order, there's no commentary regarding it. His defence is that he was just following orders. I'd like to look to see what he initially -- the position he initially took in his testimony regarding the ultimatum, and this came directly after his direct testimony, and it was in response to a question from the President. And he said: "I issued the order on the basis of a previous decision taken by the government and on the basis of the head of the Defence Department ..." And he goes on: "When you read the order, it's not an ultimatum; it's an invitation to hold discussions." And then almost 80 page -- pages later in the transcript and further in questioning from the President, the order ceases being an invitation and becomes something else. "Q. What did you envisage writing this document? The answer: "Your Honour, I did not consider this document to be any kind of ultimatum." And he goes on to explain that it's a resubordination plan. He says: "It is a reference to the provinces that do not belong, and as such, they should either be resubordinated according to this document or leave the province. Therefore, the local units, the domicile units, are both units of the ABiH and the HVO units formed there ... all the others who happen to be there and do not belong ... if they don't agree to be resubordinated to one or another party, they have to leave ..." So I would submit that by this time Petkovic's offering on this issue had changed completely. Now it was that the HVO and the ABiH's forces who were domiciled in that area could stay, but all other forces from other places had to go or be resubordinated. This is very different than his earlier testimony that it was an invitation for discussion between the HVO and the ABiH, which was his first answer. Here, the HVO and the ABiH are on the same team, and it is domicile troops against troops from the outside. It is the Prosecution's position that neither of these excuses add up to the real meaning of the ultimatum, which is an unveiled threat to the ABiH. I'd like to look at documents that were issued at the same time to shine light on this subject matter. If we can look at the next slide, which is P1135. This is a document that was issued on January 15th from Mr. Petkovic. Now, he is in Geneva with Boban at the time negotiating, yet here he issues a full combat readiness order, and in it, and these will pop up on the screen, he raises the combat level to the highest -- excuse me, I'm going to read those to you. He includes in his order all members of the Croatian people in HVO units. He does not include Muslim members. He says: "Keep only two shifts facing the Chetniks. Keep all other forces in full readiness ready to intervene towards the Muslim forces; and "Disarm and isolate all Muslims in HVO units who refuse to follow our orders." If Petkovic's 15 January order was merely a resubordination order, then these demands placed by Petkovic on the same day appear curiously inconsistent. What makes more sense is that this order was meant to tighten control and compel the Croat HVO soldiers to focus their attention on their Muslim brethren. In addition, Petkovic immediately followed up this full combat readiness order with instructions to Siljeg in Central Bosnia to stop negotiating at one hour and "fire at every move they make." It is also clear that the ABiH understood Petkovic's order to be an ultimatum, the January ultimatum, directed at the ABiH, and HVO Muslim units in the Croatian delegated provinces. In his response dated 18 January, Pasalic rote wrote this: "I cannot carry put item 2 in your order due to the fact that the 4th Corps of the Bosnian Army and its units are not under your command regarding such decisions and their execution. "The units from the 4th Corps ... will not leave the territory of the provinces you mentioned, due to the fact that the combatants in those units are inhabitants of those provinces and that they liberated those area, what was their right. To say that our units are paramilitary units is, to say the very least, not serious from your staff." It is in light of Pasalic's response, it is clearly apparent that Petkovic was dishonest with the Trial Chamber when he answered the President's unambiguous question. In addition, Pasalic's letter was written at the time of the events, a particularly persuasive factor evidencing its credibility. In contrast, Petkovic testimony is given 17 years later and is in his own defence. Well after the President's questions and pursuant to questioning from the accused Praljak, you'll see this on the next screen, he was asked about the ultimatum again, and again he says that this was an invitation to hold discussions. So so far we have gone initially from an invitation to a resubordination plan and now back to an invitation. But now when there's been time to digest the evidence and the case is closed, Petkovic finds his final defence in regards to the January ultimatum. In that defence there is no parsing of words. There's no rearranging of context or deciphering new-found issues. His explanation now is that he was just following orders. So his current position, now that the first two are found to be untenable, that he was just following orders, is contrary to the Prosecution's position, which is this: That he shared the intent of Croatian rule in the area claimed by the HVO and by issuing this order he contributed to the goal of just that. I will now turn to the Defence argument regarding who was in charge of running Petkovic's armed forces. Was it the civilians and Boban, or was it the Chief of the Main Staff, Petkovic? You will see on your monitor paragraph 3 of the brief, and this is the Defence position, which is that under the doctrine of civilian control of the military, that ultimate responsibility over strategic decision-making lies in the hands of the political civilian leadership. Here, Your Honours, we have found some common ground. Prosecution agrees that the civilian authorities were in charge of the military. Our own expert Andrew Pringle came to the same conclusion. I will now go to the Pringle report. It's paragraph 25. He says: "A range of powers would normally be vested in some form of defence council chaired by a nominated official. In the case of the HZ-HB, Article 2 of the Decree ..." which says, "The defence system of the HZ-HB shall be a uniform form of the organisation of the armed forces administrative bodies and legal entities..." And he -- Pringle concludes: "In effect, this he shrines political control over the military as one would expect." Your Honour, that is the extent of our common ground. It is then that our paths diverge. Petkovic argues that the Main Staff was so lacking in competence because most defence matters were controlled by the civilians, including, and I quote: "The competence to prescribe the authority of the Chief of the Main Staff a means available to him to prevent or punish perpetrators of the crimes," that he urges you to believe that he was not in command and control of the armed forces. Now, the Defence argument goes something like this: Petkovic says that he was in command and control of the armed forces to the extent that those powers were delegated to him by Boban. And since, his argument goes, no substantive powers were delegated to him regarding the armed forces that he was in no way responsible for them. And in specific Petkovic claims that the brigade commanders did not report to him and he was not in effective control of them. He claims in paragraph 65 that: "He was dealt with a hand that he had no way of influencing." Your Honours, the Defence would have you believe that Petkovic was a puppet of his superiors or has -- or as he goes on to write, was mere staff to Boban. And this is at paragraph 68: "The legal competence of the Chief of the Main Staff was only staff in nature (i.e., expert specialised or advisory in nature) and in regard to other specialised services specifically provided for the supreme commander. These powers did not involve any sort of command and control authority over the armed forces." Petkovic would have you believe that he was some sort of expert administrative secretary to Boban, that he had no power of his own, no ability to make any decision, no ability to control anyone below him in the organisational chart. The weight of the evidence shows that this is not the case, and Petkovic was a full-fledged former JNA officer and general in the HVO who was in charge of combat operations of the HVO and in charge of the armed forces, and in so doing significantly contributed to the JCE. The Prosecution's position was accurately articulated by Andrew Pringle, which is that the civilians managed and directed the armed forces but that Petkovic was responsible for execution of that direction and operation. And this is at paragraph 26 where Pringle writes: "The Main Staff would be responsible for performing the stipulated task in accordance with defence policy." The Defence Department and the Main Staff had separate and distinct roles. One did not exist without the other, and both were imperative to the success of the JCE. Importantly, Petkovic could not be relieved of any responsibility, because he was only following orders. He still intentionally and significantly contributed to the JCE by his own actions. The Defence argument on this is fully articulated in paragraphs 66 through 70. What is the support for this notion? It is primarily based on only two HVO legislative documents, the original decree on the armed forces and also the decision on the basic principles of organisation of the defence department. Nonetheless, even though it is based only on these two documents, the Defence brief provides an extensive examination of these documents in order to convince the Trial Chamber that no language exists supporting the Prosecution theory that Petkovic was in charge.
